newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian lumber export quotas down sharply - study.
newsitem.headline: Canadian lumber export quotas down sharply - study.

text.p: Canadian lumber mills have been allocated export quotas to the United States that are as much as 40 percent below their 1995 shipments, according to a study Wednesday.

Widman's World Wood Review, an industry newsletter, released the findings after surveying a sampling of mills in British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario and Quebec. Among mills surveyed, those in Quebec said their duty-free export quota to the United States was 60 to 65 percent of actual 1995 shipments. In Ontario the figure was 60 to 70 percent, Alberta 65 to 70 percent and British Columbia 75 to 85 percent.

Under a trade deal between Canada and the United States reached earlier this year, Canadian lumber exports are capped at 14.7 billion board feet. Above that level, exporters must pay a duty. The level was about 10 percent below 1995's actual shipments of around 16.2 billion board feet.
But Canadian mills who were allocated their individual duty-free allowances by the government last month have widely complained that the amounts were drastically below 1995.
"The question is, where did the quotas go? That's what everyone is asking," said Charles Widman, publisher of the newsletter.

While the mills with the most generous quotas received 85 percent of 1995 shipments, no one in the survey received the 90 percent that would have been expected under the deal's plan to cut exports by about 10 percent, Widman said.
"It's an administrative nightmare, an absolute disaster," he said.

Many producers in Ontario and Quebec have used virtually all their duty free quota for the year running to next April. "They will have to decide either to pay the penalty (duty) or shut down," Widman said.
